銅鈸多成對使用，演奏者以穿過鈸心孔的帶子手持，或將單片懸掛於支架。基本發聲是兩片: Cymbals are mostly used in pairs: the player holds them by a strap through the central hole, or hangs a single plate on a stand. The basic sound is one plate struck against the other, and they can also be struck with a drumstick; begin by practising a steady grip and using different parts of the plate: sliding the edges together for a hiss, clashing them for a crash, tapping the edge of one lightly against the face of the other for a light splash, scraping from the bell out to the edge for a scrape, and pressing them together for a choked sound. Damping can be done by holding the cymbal close to the body, and the score and the context decide it. The force needs control, since everything from very light to very loud has its use.
銅鈸屬體鳴樂器，多以成對薄圓盤互擊發聲，可聽於交響樂團、打擊樂合奏、爵士樂團、搖: Cymbals are idiophones, mostly played as a pair of thin round plates struck together, and can be heard in symphony orchestras, percussion ensembles, jazz bands, rock bands and marching bands; a drum kit usually holds a crash, a ride and a pair of hi-hats. In the orchestra, cymbals are used in Wagner's Tannhäuser, Grieg's Peer Gynt, Mozart's The Abduction from the Seraglio, Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, Stravinsky's Petrushka and Mahler's Titan Symphony. Cymbals are also used in Indian temples and in the Ganges rituals, in the Iranian Ashura ceremony and in Turkish janissary music.

They are made as thin round plates, mostly of copper alloy, drilled at the centre so that they can be fixed to a stand or held on a strap; they are usually used in pairs, and can also be struck with a drumstick. Most cymbals have no definite pitch, though a few small cymbals of ancient design can sound a fixed note. A player is called a cymbalist, and cymbals are common in symphony orchestras and percussion ensembles.

Cymbals are a common percussion instrument, Hornbostel-Sachs number 111.142, an idiophone found in Asia, the Middle East and Europe. They are made as thin round plates, mostly of copper alloy, drilled at the centre so that they can be fixed to a stand or held on a strap; they are usually used in pairs, and can also be struck with a drumstick. Most cymbals have no definite pitch, though a few small cymbals of ancient design can sound a fixed note. A player is called a cymbalist, and cymbals are common in symphony orchestras, percussion ensembles, jazz bands, rock bands and marching bands; a jazz drum kit usually has at least a crash, a ride or a crash/ride, and a pair of hi-hats.
銅鈸為體鳴樂器，以薄圓盤相互撞擊或受敲擊發聲。多數銅鈸音高不確定，小型依早期設計: Cymbals are idiophones, sounded by thin round plates struck against each other or struck. Most have no definite pitch, though small ones of early design can have a fixed note; the bell sounds higher and a thin cymbal lower. Bigger cymbals usually mean more volume and a longer sustain; heavier ones are louder and carry further, while thinner ones respond faster. Volume and timbre can be controlled by clashing, scraping, damping against the body or striking with a drumstick. Within the family, the crash is thinner with more damping and suits clashing; the ride and the hi-hat are thicker with less damping and suit a steady rhythm.
銅鈸的發聲體為薄圓盤，來源僅載明由各種銅合金製成，未列具體合金成分。中心鑽孔，用: The sounding body of the cymbal is a thin round plate; the sources say only that it is made of various copper alloys and do not list the exact composition. A hole is drilled in the centre to mount it on a stand or to thread a strap through for holding by hand; the sources mention that leather straps or rope can be used for hanging, and that modern drum hardware also uses felt or other damping cloth as an isolating material. The materials of the other parts, such as stands, drumsticks and fixings, are not recorded in the sources.
銅鈸自古存在，亞美尼亞高原、拉爾薩、巴比倫、亞述、古埃及、古希臘與古羅馬均有浮雕: Cymbals have existed since ancient times: reliefs and paintings from the Armenian highlands, Larsa, Babylon, Assyria, ancient Egypt, ancient Greece and ancient Rome show them, and the Bible mentions them often. They may have come into China from Central Asia in the 3rd or 4th century AD. India has used them since ancient times in temples and Buddhist sites, and large cymbals appear in the Ganges rituals. Persian epics of about 977 and 1010 mention cymbals many times, for the din of war and for celebration, and call them Indian cymbals; in the Ashura ceremony, striking stones was later replaced by cymbals and other instruments. The Turkish janissaries used them before the 14th century, they entered European music in the 17th century, were common in military bands and orchestras by the middle of the 18th, and their uses widened after the 19th.
